concept.name: Test of spring
concept.definition: The Wyckoff event in which price revisits the low of a spring or shakeout to verify that supply is exhausted. A successful test makes a higher low (or holds near the spring low) on clearly lower volume, indicating the stock is ready for markup.
concept.intuition: After the fake breakdown, the market dips once more to double-check that no sellers remain; a quiet, low-volume dip passes the check.
concept.mechanics: Large operators repeatedly test the market for supply; after a spring, one or more tests revisit the spring low. The analyst compares volume and spread with the spring: a successful test shows significantly less volume and holds at or above the spring low, and is treated as a confirmation to initiate or add to long positions.
concept.failure_modes: A test on volume that is not meaningfully lower, or one that undercuts the spring low decisively, negates the bullish reading; tests can also be repeated many times, delaying or preventing markup.
concept.misconceptions: The test does not need to exactly match the spring low, and a single successful test is not an absolute guarantee; it is one piece of evidence weighed with the sign of strength that should follow.
concept.example: After a spring to 87, a stock drifts back to 89 on the lightest volume in months and closes unchanged; the trader buys a partial position, treating it as a successful test of the spring.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
